claims.text: Crystal-structure selection in noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by the balance between rapid heating and the cooling rate.
A sufficiently rapid quench kinetically locks in a metastable single-phase solid solution.
A modest reduction in cooling rate increases atomic mobility.
The increased atomic mobility caused by slower cooling promotes elemental segregation and phase separation.
Differences in constituent-element diffusion kinetics during cooling mediate nucleation and growth and thereby influence phase uniformity.
Suppressing diffusion during rapid quenching kinetically traps a metastable single-phase structure.
Enhanced diffusion during slower cooling produces elemental segregation, phase separation, or secondary phases that disrupt the solid solution.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a uniform single-phase crystal structure.
Moderately cooled nanoparticles will exhibit detectable elemental aggregation and distinct secondary phases.
Moderated cooling may alter nanoparticle morphology and cause phase separation in some particles.
Rapid heating followed by ultra-rapid cooling typically yields metastable single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Compositions extending beyond noble metals or substantially different heating regimes may fall outside the mechanism's applicability.
